Why are you sat here all alone? Where is your mother and your brothers and sisters? The baby duck hopped into the canoe and sat between Zach and his cat. I think he wants some company, Sydney. Maybe we will see his family along the river somewhere. They paddled back up the river toward the bridge again. Keep your eyes open, Sydney, said Zach. His family must be around here somewhere. The little duck sat next to Sydney and watched the swans float past. As they floated under the bridge, they saw a mother goose with her babies. "That's not your mommy," said Zach to the baby duck. "Don't worry, we will find her." Look, there is your mommy and your brothers and sisters. We found them. The baby duck flapped his little wings with excitement. The baby duck was so happy to find his family, he gave Zach the biggest hug he could manage to say thank you. Then he jumped into the water and swam to meet his mother, who was overjoyed to see her little lost one. "What a great day we had on the river, Sydney," said Zach. "I'm so glad we could help that little duck find his family. It feels good to help others." Sydney purred and smiled in agreement.

title: Master Thistlewhisk's Halloween
description: The story of master THistlewhisk and a runaway pumpkin.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Master Thistlewisk's Halloween. On a dewy morning late in October, Master Thistlewisk was out in the meadow at the edge of the woods picking fresh field mushrooms. He always liked to pick them early as they popped up overnight, and so the dawn picking was always the freshest. As he walked along the edge of the stream, he met a friend of his, Holly the Hedgehog. She was carrying a bucket of water out of the front door of her burrow. He greeted her with a smile. Good day to you, Holly. Are you keeping well? I have fresh rose hip syrup if you or your little ones are in need. Thank you kindly, Master Thistlewisk. What I need most right now is a dry home. The stream rose overnight and we were all ankled deep at the breakfast table. "Oh dear, I am sorry to hear this." He shook his head. "Take these mushrooms, Holly. You can make a warming soup for you and the family, and I will pass by tomorrow with a bottle of rose hip syrup. That will keep you all healthy through these damp days." Master Thistlewisk continued on his foraging walk. And at the far end of the meadow, at the edge of the woods, he stopped to gather fallen sweet chestnuts to roast on the fire. He could hear horses hooves clipclopping loudly as they passed by on the lane above. As the cart rolled by, a wheel hit a big stone in the lane and three giant pumpkins came rolling off the back of the cart and came to a halt in the grass near the tree. He stood for a few moments, staring at the pumpkins. Then a wonderful idea struck him. Using all his strength, Master Thistlewisk rolled the giant pumpkins to a beautiful fur tree in a quiet spot in the woods. Master Thistlewisk had a plan. He set to work at once. He brought all the materials he needed from his workshop at home. After four long days of hard work, Master Thawisk stood back and admired his creation. It was beautiful. Master Thistlewisk knocked at Holly's door. "Hello, Holly," he said. "Come with me. Bring the family. I want to show you something." Master Thistlewisk had made this house especially for a friend of his. It is for you, Holly, so you don't get flooded by the stream anymore. Holly was overjoyed and quite overcome at her friend's generosity. Oh, Master Thistlewisk, you must be our first dinner guest as we celebrate our new home. I'd be delighted, Holly, he nodded. On the night of Halloween, Master Thistlewisk had supper with Holly and her family. They enjoyed creamy mushroom soup and drank some particularly delicious elderflower cordial Master Thistlewisk had brought with him.

title: Arabella Loses her Cat
description: Adventures in the Whispering Wood with Arabella, her cat Fluffy and Master Thistlewhisk.

At the very edge of the whispering wood, where the ferns grew thick and the sunlight danced through the trees, there stood a little stone cottage. In front of the cottage stretched the most beautiful garden in all the forest. It was full of neat rows of vegetables, their green leaves standing proudly in the morning light, plump carrots, shiny beetroot, and lettucees as crisp as spring rain. Between them grew beds of flowers and herbs, golden calundula, lavender, thyme, comfrey, and sage. The air was always rich with their scent. At the far end of the garden, a clear little stream wound its way between smooth stones. its song mingling with the hum of bees and the soft couping of wood pigeons. Dragonflies shimmerred over the water, and the rabbit often said the stream kept his garden happy and his heart calm. This was the home of Master Thistlewisk, a wise old white rabbit. Master Thistlewisk was no ordinary rabbit. He was the herbalist and healer of the forest. Every bird, hedgehog, squirrel, and fox who lived nearby knew that if they ever scraped a wing or caught a chill, they could hop, scamper, or flutter to Master Thistlewisk's cottage, and he would make them well again. One bright morning, the rabbit straightened his brown jacket, took a small pouch into his pocket, and set out into the forest. He was searching for wild wood sorrel, a soft green herb that grew in the cool shaded glades. It was excellent for easing upset stomachs, and he was running low. He hummed a tune as he went, pausing to sniff the air, and listened to the distant songs of finches. When he found the sorrel, its clover-shaped leaves sparkled with dew. Master Thistlewisk smiled. "Ah, perfect," he said to himself. but only as much as I can carry. He plucked a few handfuls gently, careful not to disturb the roots, and left plenty behind. That was his rule, always leave enough for others to use and enjoy. As he turned to head home, he noticed something unusual. Just ahead on a mossy tree stump sat a little girl. Her face was pinched with worry, and her hands were clasped tightly in her lap. Why, Miss Arabella? Master Thistlewisk exclaimed, recognizing her at once. Whatever's the matter, my dear. Arabella looked up, startled to see the talking rabbit in his brown jacket, though she had met him once before when her mother's roses needed help recovering from mildew. "Oh, Master Thistlewisk," she sniffled. "I've lost Fluffy. We were picking berries for a pie, but she ran off into the woods, and now I can't find her anywhere. The rabbit's nose twitched kindly. "Oh, that does sound troublesome, but don't you fret, young miss. Cats are clever creatures, and I dare say she hasn't gone too far." Arabella blinked away her tears. "Do you really think so?" I do indeed, said Master Thistlewisk, patting her hand with his soft paw. Now, let's try calling her together. Sometimes the forest needs to be reminded to listen. So, Arabella stood up, cuped her hand to her mouth, and called out as loud as she could, "Fluffy! Fluffy! Where are you? Come back, please." For a moment there was only the rustle of leaves and the chatter of a distant magpie. But then just faintly came a familiar meow. From somewhere behind a bramble bush. Fluffy, Arabella cried. She ran toward the sound and out from the ferns bounded a black and white cat with big blue eyes and a dusty tail. She leapt straight into Arabella's arms, purring so loudly it sounded like a tiny engine. "Oh, Fluffy, I was so worried," Arabella said, hugging her tight. "Meow," said Fluffy, blinking apologetically. "I saw a mouse and had to chase it, but then it disappeared down a hole, and I didn't know how to get back." Master Thistlewisk chuckled. A common enough problem, young miss," he said to the cat. "The forest can be confusing when one follows one's whiskers instead of one's sense." "Ara g" giggled, and even Fluffy gave a small rumbling purr of agreement. "Now," said the rabbit, brushing a leaf off his jacket. "Since we're all safely together again, how about I walk you both home? Evening will be here before long, and I know the forest paths better than most." So the three of them walked together through the dappled woods. By the time they reached Arabella's garden gate, the sky had turned golden pink. "Thank you, Master Thistlewisk," said Arabella. "You're ever so kind." "The rabbit bowed slightly. Think nothing of it, my dear. And if ever you'd like to learn more about the healing plants of the forest, my garden gate is always open. Come visit me, and I'll teach you all I know. Arabella smiled. I will, I promise. Fluffy purred in agreement, though she was already dreaming of a saucer of milk and a nap by the fire. Master Thistlewisk tipped his ear in farewell and hopped down the path toward his cottage. That night, if you had peered through the trees, you might have seen the gentle glow of lamplight through the window of his stone cottage. Smoke curled from the crooked chimney, rising into a starfleckle sky. The moon shone silver over the garden, where fireflies drifted like tiny lanterns. An owl sat on a nearby branch, watching over the peaceful forest. And inside, Master Thistlewisk sipped chamomile tea, humming softly as he packed away his freshly gathered sorrel, content as always to know that all was well in the whispering wood,

title: Master Thistlewhisk and the praying mantis

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Master Thistlewisk and the praying mantis. On the edge of an ancient whispering forest, there stood a little stone cottage. Around the cottage stretched a garden unlike any other, a patchwork quilt of herbs, vegetables, wild flowers, and berry bushes. The caretaker of this wondrous place was none other than a gentle white rabbit known to all the animals far and wide as Master Thistlewhis, the healer of the woods. Master Thistlewisk spent his days tending to his herbs, lavender, chamomile, peppermint, sage, and countless others. He knew the secret of each leaf and root. And when a fox caught a thorn in its paw or a sparrow grew weak with fever, it was the rabbit's remedies that brought comfort and healing. All who came to his garden found not only medicine, but also kindness. But nestled quietly among the tall stems of fennel in one corner of the garden lived another creature, one far less known, but just as remarkable. She was a preying mantis named Merrila, slender and green as a new spring leaf. One day, as she peered out from her hiding place, she watched a squirrel with a scraped tail hop into the garden. Master Thistlewisk, bent low, cleaned the wound, and wrapped it with a soft leaf. The squirrel squeaked with gratitude before bounding off, his tail safely bandaged. Merilla tilted her head thoughtfully. "How noble," she whispered to herself. "The rabbit brings healing to all. But what of me? I too wish to be of use. Am I only to hide among the fennel forever? A butterfly ellighted on a nearby flower and overheard her musings. Perhaps you simply have not yet discovered your gift, the butterfly said kindly. Merilla sighed. But what could a mantis offer? My legs are sharp, my eyes strange, and my hunger frightens others. I fear they would never welcome me. Still the thought lingered in her heart. Perhaps she had a role yet to play. Late one summer afternoon, trouble stirred. Dark clouds gathered over the ancient forest, and with them came a swarm of hungry beetles. They marched from tree to tree, devouring leaves, stripping branches bare. Soon they reached the garden's edge, their numbers so vast they made the ground tremble. Master Thistlewisk looked on with worry. If these beetles reach my herbs, the medicines for the animals will be ruined. The fox, the deer, and the sparrows all freted. None knew how to stop the swarm. Merilla watched silently from the fennel. Her heart beat fast. She knew beetles well. She had hunted them before. Alone she could catch only a few, but this was a plague too great even for her swift four legs. Still she could not turn away. At last she whispered, "Perhaps this is the moment my gift will be revealed." With sudden courage, Merrila climbed to the tallest fennel stalk and called out in a clear ringing voice. Friends of the garden, do not despair. I will face the beetles. The animals gasped, for most had never noticed the mantis before, but Master Thistlewisk's wise eyes glowed with hope. The beetles surged into the garden, gnoring at leaves and stems. Merrila leapt into their midst, her slender body swaying like a reed. She spread her four legs wide and began to move in a strange rhythmic dance. The Beatles paused. Her motions were mesmerizing, slow, graceful, yet commanding. They watched, spellbound, forgetting their hunger. She pivoted and swayed, her eyes gleaming like emerald fire. One by one, the Beatles faltered, dazed by the spectacle. Then, with a sudden flick, she darted forward and seized the boldest of them. The others shrieked and scuttled back. Again she danced. Again she struck until the swarm broke into chaos. At last the beetles fled, tumbling over each other in their haste to escape the enchantment of the mantis. Silence fell over the garden. The plants, though nibbled, still stood strong. The animals stared in awe at Merilla. Master Thistlewisk hopped forward, his whiskers twitching with joy. Merilla, brave one, you have saved the garden. Your dance was a wonder, a shield stronger than any wall. The animals cheered, their voices rising like bird song. The sparrows swooped low to bow their heads. The deer bent their necks, and the fox wagged his bushy tail. Mela's heart swelled with warmth she had never felt before. For the first time, she was not hidden or overlooked. She was seen. She was needed. She was cherished. The white rabbit smiled kindly. Each creature has its gift, though it may not be known at once. Yours, Merrila, is both courage and grace. the power to protect through fearlessness and beauty. From that day on, Merilla was no longer the hidden mantis of the fenneltoalk. She became the guardian of the garden, watching over the herbs and flowers with her patient stillness and her fierce dance when danger approached. The seasons turned as they always do. In autumn, Merrila watched the rabbit gather roots and dry herbs, and she perched beside him to ward off any pests. In winter, when the snow blanketed the garden, she rested within the cottage, listening to Master Thistlewisk tell stories to the animals huddled near the fire. In spring, she joined the rabbit in welcoming new blooms, marveling at the colors and scents that returned with warmth. And in summer she basked once more on her fennel stalk, eyes ever watchful. She was no longer lonely, for she had found her place, and she knew that even the smallest, quietest creature could hold a gift as grand as any healer's herb. And so in the garden on the edge of the ancient forest, peace and harmony thrived, guarded by a white rabbit with healing paws and a praying mantis with a dancing heart.
